agenda: Maintenance of international peace and security
members: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland

steps.intent: Guyana's primary objectives as penholder are to maintain the objective monthly reporting mandate under resolution 2722 (2024), secure the release of the Galaxy Leader crew, and integrate previously overlooked priorities, specifically the environmental risks of maritime attacks and the protection of humanitarian aid delivery. The most contentious negotiation points are expected to be the explicit framing of regional root causes and restraint, which must be carefully calibrated to satisfy Western members (the US and UK) without triggering a veto from Russia or China, while ensuring references to environmental impacts and humanitarian assistance gain consensus.

messages.Algeria: Algeria appreciates the initiative taken by Guyana and Sierra Leone and reiterates its firm commitment to maritime security, freedom of navigation, and the safety of seafarers. However, to achieve a balanced and effective text, the Council must be objective by explicitly acknowledging the catastrophic situation in Gaza as a key driver of regional escalation and ensure that measures undertaken do not serve as a pretext to violate the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Yemen.
messages.China: China appreciates the efforts of Guyana and Sierra Leone in preparing this draft and shares concerns over maritime safety in the Red Sea and the disruption to international trade routes. However, resolution of the Red Sea crisis requires a comprehensive approach addressing root causes, de-escalating military confrontations, and respecting Yemen's sovereignty and territorial integrity. We urge the penholders to incorporate language ensuring Council resolutions are not abused to justify unauthorized military strikes, and we look forward to working constructively on the text.
messages.Denmark: Denmark thanks Guyana and Sierra Leone for taking the initiative on this timely draft and strongly supports extending the reporting mandate under resolution 2722. As a leading maritime nation, we emphasize that Council action must remain consistent with established language by reaffirming the right of Member States to defend vessels in accordance with international law and by addressing the flow of weapons to the Houthis through the strict enforcement of the arms embargo. We stand ready to engage constructively to ensure the draft sends an unambiguous message in defense of freedom of navigation.
messages.France: France thanks Guyana and Sierra Leone for circulating this draft to extend the reporting mandate and maintain the Council's firm stance against Houthi attacks in the Red Sea. To preserve the legal and operational coherence established in resolution 2722 (2024), it is essential that the text explicitly recognizes the right of States to defend vessels under international law and calls for strict adherence to the arms embargo. We look forward to working constructively with the co-sponsors to incorporate these necessary elements.
messages.Greece: Greece thanks Guyana and Sierra Leone for putting forward this draft extending the vital reporting mechanism established by resolution 2722. As a leading maritime nation and co-penholder on previous resolutions on this file, we strongly emphasize the imperative of protecting international shipping, securing the release of all innocent seafarers, and reaffirming the right of States under international law to defend their vessels against unlawful attacks. We look forward to working constructively to finalize this text.
messages.Pakistan: Pakistan welcomes this balanced draft circulated by Guyana and Sierra Leone, which reflects our consistent commitment to freedom of navigation, maritime safety, and addressing the root causes of regional instability. As emphasized in our national statements, it is essential that all international responses adhere strictly to international law and the UN Charter to prevent broader regional spillover. We strongly support the extension of the reporting mandate and look forward to working constructively toward the adoption of this resolution.
messages.Panama: Panama strongly welcomes this draft resolution circulated by Guyana and Sierra Leone. As a major maritime nation and flag State committed to the security of international navigation and global supply chains, we fully endorse the continuation of the reporting mandate and the condemnation of unlawful attacks against commercial vessels. We propose a minor addition to operational paragraph 2 to highlight the protection of civilian seafarers who face grave risks from these attacks.
messages.Republic of Korea: The Republic of Korea appreciates Guyana and Sierra Leone's initiative to maintain Council engagement on the critical situation in the Red Sea. As a major trading and maritime nation, safeguarding the freedom of navigation and the safety of commercial shipping is of vital national interest to us. To ensure this text remains effective and aligned with resolution 2722 (2024) and subsequent renewals, it is essential to reaffirm the targeted arms embargo under resolution 2216 (2015) and recognize Member States' right to defend their vessels in accordance with international law.
messages.Russian Federation: The Russian Federation consistently supports ensuring the safety of maritime navigation in the Red Sea, but the current text remains fundamentally one-sided. It completely ignores the ongoing, illegal military strikes against sovereign Yemeni territory conducted by the Western coalition, which are spuriously justified using misinterpretations of resolution 2722 (2024). Furthermore, any realistic effort to de-escalate maritime tensions must explicitly recognize the root cause of regional instability, namely the catastrophic situation in the Gaza Strip.
messages.Sierra Leone: As a co-sponsor of this draft resolution alongside Guyana, Sierra Leone fully supports the text as presented. The draft strikes a balanced and necessary approach by firmly condemning attacks on commercial vessels, extending the vital reporting mandate, and addressing critical humanitarian, environmental, and regional de-escalation concerns. We urge all Council members to support this draft to uphold maritime security and international law with a unified voice.
messages.Slovenia: Slovenia warmly welcomes this draft and commends Guyana and Sierra Leone for incorporating strong language on the protection of the marine environment, which has been a longstanding priority for our delegation. As a maritime country, freedom of navigation and the safety of commercial shipping routes remain paramount. To address the ongoing attacks effectively, we ask the penholders to include a clear call for the full implementation of the targeted arms embargo under resolutions 2140 (2014) and 2216 (2015).
messages.Somalia: Somalia welcomes the initiative taken by Guyana and Sierra Leone and strongly supports the draft's objectives to protect maritime navigation, mitigate environmental risks, and de-escalate tensions. As a coastal State in the region, Somalia underscores that lasting maritime security must center on the primary role and responsibility of Red Sea littoral States alongside international cooperation. We look forward to working constructively with the co-sponsors to reflect this important regional dimension in the text.
messages.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: The United Kingdom welcomes Guyana's initiative to maintain Council focus on the reckless and illegal Houthi attacks against international shipping in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden. To ensure consistency with resolution 2722 (2024), it is essential that the Council reaffirms the right of Member States to defend vessels against these unlawful attacks and addresses the illicit flow of weapons enabling them. We look forward to working constructively with the penholders to incorporate these established agreed elements.
messages.United States of America: The United States welcomes the initiative by Guyana and Sierra Leone to extend the reporting mandate and condemn ongoing Houthi maritime attacks. However, it is essential that this Council does not dilute the established framework of resolution 2722 (2024), specifically the reaffirmation of Member States' right to defend their vessels against these attacks in accordance with international law. We must also explicitly address the illegal arms flows, facilitated by Iran in direct violation of resolution 2216 (2015), that enable these continuous threats to freedom of navigation and innocent mariners.

steps.summary: As co-penholder, Guyana revised the draft to bridge key divides by accepting the US red line on the right of Member States to defend vessels (OP2) while accommodating Russia's red line clarifying that the resolution does not authorize armed force against Yemen (OP6). The revision also integrates broad calls from elected and permanent members to address the root causes including the Gaza conflict, enforce the targeted arms embargo, protect seafarers, and uphold the sovereignty of coastal States.

messages.Algeria: Algeria expresses its deep appreciation to Guyana and Sierra Leone for addressing our core concerns in Revision 1, notably by explicitly acknowledging the situation in Gaza and the necessity of an immediate ceasefire, while firmly safeguarding the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Yemen. The clear parameters established in OP5 and OP6 effectively counter the misuse of the principle of self-defence to justify military strikes on sovereign territory. Algeria fully supports the draft text in its current form and encourages Council members to preserve this well-balanced compromise.
messages.China: China appreciates the penholders' efforts to balance the draft by incorporating our proposals regarding the UN Charter, the Gaza ceasefire, and limits on the use of force. To fully address our core concerns and prevent further escalation, the resolution must explicitly emphasize that Council resolutions should not be misinterpreted or abused, and demand an end to attacks on Yemeni civilian infrastructure. Incorporating this language into paragraph 5 will be vital for China's final position on the draft.
messages.Denmark: Denmark appreciates the penholders' constructive approach and welcomes the incorporation of our proposals on defending vessels, the arms embargo, and the release of the MV Galaxy Leader and its crew. However, we have strong concerns regarding OP6, which is redundant given the safeguards already outlined in OP5 and risks creating legal ambiguity regarding the inherent right of self-defence under international law. Furthermore, while Denmark supports diplomatic efforts and de-escalation across the region, PP8 should reflect agreed language from resolution 2722 (2024) to avoid any perception of legitimizing or linking illegal attacks on commercial shipping to other regional conflicts.
messages.France: France thanks Guyana and Sierra Leone for constructively taking into account our proposals in Revision 1, particularly regarding the right of Member States to defend vessels in accordance with international law, the targeted arms embargo under resolution 2216 (2015), and the demand for the release of the MV Galaxy Leader and its crew. To ensure a balanced text, we suggest a minor addition to PP8 to make clear that, while diplomatic efforts and a ceasefire in Gaza are essential to de-escalate regional tensions, no crisis can serve as a pretext or justification for attacks against commercial navigation. With this balanced adjustment, France is prepared to fully support the adoption of the draft resolution.
messages.Greece: Greece thanks the co-penholders, Guyana and Sierra Leone, for constructively accommodating our proposals in the revised draft, particularly the explicit recognition of Member States' right to defend vessels in accordance with international law and the urgent demand for the release of all unlawfully detained seafarers. As a pre-eminent maritime nation deeply committed to the safety of seafarers, freedom of navigation, and international law as reflected in UNCLOS, Greece fully supports the draft resolution in its current form. We encourage all Council members to unite behind this text to ensure maritime security and the protection of vital global supply chains.
messages.Pakistan: Pakistan appreciates the penholders' constructive engagement and welcomes the inclusion of language in operative paragraph 5 emphasizing caution, restraint, and strict adherence to the UN Charter and international law, including the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Yemen. The draft text strikes an appropriate balance by upholding the safety of commercial navigation and addressing the root causes of regional tensions, including the urgent need for a ceasefire in Gaza. Pakistan is pleased to support the draft resolution in its current form.
messages.Panama: Panama thanks the co-sponsors for incorporating our language regarding the safety, protection, and well-being of all merchant mariners and seafarers into operative paragraph 3. As a leading maritime nation and flag State, Panama fully supports this draft resolution, which defends freedom of navigation under international law and UNCLOS, safeguards global supply chains, and protects mariners. We are prepared to vote in favour of the text as currently drafted.
messages.Republic of Korea: The Republic of Korea thanks the penholders for constructively incorporating all our proposals into Revision 1, notably regarding the right of Member States to defend vessels, the release of the MV Galaxy Leader and its crew, and strict adherence to the targeted arms embargo. The draft effectively addresses the vital necessity of safeguarding maritime security, the freedom of navigation, and regional stability in the Red Sea. We are prepared to support the draft resolution in its current form.
messages.Russian Federation: We appreciate the penholders' constructive effort in incorporating our red line regarding the non-authorization of the use of force in operative paragraph 6, as well as addressing the root cause in Gaza. Nevertheless, operative paragraph 2 retains the flawed formulation from resolution 2722 (2024), which has been cynically exploited by the United States and the United Kingdom as a cover for their illegal airstrikes against sovereign Yemeni territory. Deleting OP2 and clearly demanding a halt to these unauthorized military actions in OP5 are essential steps to make this text genuinely balanced and prevent further dangerous regional escalation.
messages.Sierra Leone: As a co-sponsor of this draft resolution, Sierra Leone fully supports the text as presented in Revision 1. The draft achieves a balanced and comprehensive approach by condemning attacks against commercial vessels, protecting navigational rights and seafarer safety, addressing the severe ecological and humanitarian consequences, and emphasizing the necessity of tackling root causes and preventing broader regional escalation. We urge all Council members to support this text to maintain Council unity on this critical international peace and security issue.
messages.Slovenia: Slovenia thanks Guyana and Sierra Leone for their constructive leadership and for incorporating our concerns regarding the targeted arms embargo into OP4. We also warmly welcome the inclusion of strong language on maritime environmental protection and the call for regional de-escalation, which align closely with our national priorities as a maritime nation. Slovenia is satisfied with the current balanced text and is prepared to vote in favour.
messages.Somalia: Somalia extends its sincere appreciation to Guyana and Sierra Leone for accommodating our priority by incorporating PP3, affirming the primary responsibility of coastal and littoral States in ensuring Red Sea maritime security. The current draft strikes an essential balance between safeguarding navigational rights, upholding state sovereignty, and addressing the root causes and environmental perils in our shared waters. Somalia is pleased to offer its full support to the draft resolution in its current form.
messages.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: We welcome the penholder's incorporation of our language on the right of Member States to defend their vessels and on compliance with the targeted arms embargo. However, operative paragraph 6 is unacceptable as it attempts to distort the legal framework governing lawful action in self-defence under international law and Article 51 of the Charter. Furthermore, preambular paragraph 8 must not validate Houthi narratives by drawing a false linkage between illegal maritime attacks and the situation in Gaza; we urge a return to agreed Security Council language.
messages.United States of America: The United States appreciates the penholders' incorporation of our core priorities regarding the inherent right of Member States to defend their vessels and strict enforcement of the targeted arms embargo. However, we cannot accept PP8, which legitimizes the Houthis' false pretext linking their reckless attacks on civilian shipping to the conflict in Gaza; this text must return to the agreed formulation of resolution 2722 (2024). Furthermore, OP6 is unacceptable as it attempts to retroactively re-interpret prior Council resolutions and constrain lawful actions taken in self-defense.

steps.summary: As penholder, Guyana adjusted Revision 1 to resolve the red lines of the United States and the United Kingdom by deleting OP6 and reverting PP8 to agreed Security Council language from resolution 2722 (2024), thereby averting potential vetoes. OP5 was constructively updated to partially accommodate Chinese concerns regarding the protection of civilian infrastructure and adherence to Council mandates. The draft successfully preserves Guyana's priorities on reporting renewal, environmental protection, and humanitarian assistance, ensuring strong adoption prospects with zero negative votes.

reasons.Algeria: Algeria voted in favour of the draft resolution co-authored by fellow A3+ member Sierra Leone and Guyana, as it successfully incorporates crucial safeguards regarding the respect for Yemen's sovereignty and territorial integrity, urges restraint, and explicitly warns against the misuse or misinterpretation of Security Council resolutions to justify strikes on sovereign territory.
reasons.China: Consistent with China's established voting record on resolutions 2722, 2739, 2768, and 2787, China abstains due to lingering concerns over the potential misinterpretation and military misuse of provisions related to defending vessels against attacks, while reserving its remarks for an explanation of vote after the adoption.
reasons.Denmark: As a major seafaring nation committed to freedom of navigation and maritime security in the Red Sea, Denmark strongly supports this resolution, especially since our key negotiation requests were fully incorporated by the penholders.
reasons.France: France consistently supports the maintenance of maritime security and freedom of navigation in the Red Sea, firmly condemning Houthi attacks in line with our votes on resolutions 2722, 2739, 2768, and 2787. Although our suggested minor addition to the preambular text was not fully incorporated, the draft retains essential provisions upholding international law and vessel defense rights, warranting an affirmative vote.
reasons.Greece: As a major maritime nation and prior co-penholder on this file, Greece steadfastly supports the draft resolution's robust condemnation of Houthi attacks, protection of seafarers, defense of freedom of navigation under UNCLOS, and extension of the UN reporting mechanism. Greece reserves its remarks for after the vote.
reasons.Guyana: As the lead sponsor of the draft resolution alongside Sierra Leone, Guyana will naturally vote in favour of its own text and takes the floor before the vote to introduce the draft and urge Council members to support it.
reasons.Pakistan: Pakistan consistently supports the protection of commercial shipping and maritime security in the Red Sea while advocating for de-escalation, adherence to international law, and addressing root causes, all of which are adequately reflected in the balanced draft text.
reasons.Panama: As a major maritime nation and flag state, Panama consistently supports Security Council action to protect navigational rights, international shipping lanes, and the safety of seafarers in accordance with UNCLOS and international law. The draft resolution directly addresses these core priorities and extends the critical reporting mechanism under resolution 2722 (2024).
reasons.Republic of Korea: The draft resolution aligns directly with the Republic of Korea's national interests as a major maritime trading nation by upholding freedom of navigation in the Red Sea, condemning unlawful Houthi attacks, and reinforcing the targeted arms embargo under resolution 2216 (2015).
reasons.Russian Federation: In line with our consistent position on resolutions 2722, 2739, 2768, and 2787, Russia abstains because the text retains problematic language in paragraph 2 regarding the defense of vessels—which has been abused by the US-led coalition to justify illegal strikes on Yemen—while our proposed amendments to halt unauthorized military action were rejected.
reasons.Sierra Leone: As a co-sponsor of the draft resolution with Guyana and consistent with our prior votes on resolutions 2722, 2739, 2768, and 2787, Sierra Leone votes in favour to uphold maritime security, international law, and the safety of seafarers.
reasons.Slovenia: Slovenia consistently supports the renewal of reporting mandates on Red Sea security, the protection of freedom of navigation, compliance with the arms embargo, and environmental risk mitigation, aligning fully with its established maritime and foreign policy priorities.
reasons.Somalia: Somalia consistently supports resolutions safeguarding maritime security and freedom of navigation in the Red Sea, especially with the draft explicitly emphasizing the primary responsibility of coastal and littoral States and respect for territorial integrity. Following our standard practice in previous adoptions on this item, we vote in favour and reserve our statement for after the vote.
reasons.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: The draft resolution maintains essential language condemning Houthi attacks, upholds the right of Member States to defend vessels under international law, extends the reporting mandate under resolution 2722, and accommodated our key negotiation priorities.
reasons.United States of America: The draft resolution incorporates our key red lines and requested changes, maintains strong condemnation of Houthi maritime attacks, reinforces the arms embargo under resolution 2216, demands the release of detained crews including from the MV Eternity C, and extends vital reporting through July 2026.

before.Guyana:
Guyana has the honour to present the draft resolution before the Security Council today, co-sponsored with Sierra Leone, which seeks to extend the reporting mandate established under resolution 2722 (2024) through 15 July 2026.

As an elected member of this Council and an ardent defender of international law, including the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, Guyana has consistently affirmed that the Council must act decisively to uphold international peace, maritime security, and freedom of navigation. Continued attacks against commercial and merchant vessels in the Red Sea and surrounding waterways pose grave risks to maritime trade, the safety of innocent seafarers, and the fragile marine environment. 

In crafting this text, our delegation sought to bridge perspectives across this Council by presenting a balanced, comprehensive, and fact-based approach. The draft resolution not only demands an immediate cessation of all Houthi attacks and the unconditional release of unlawfully detained seafarers—including the crews of the *MV Galaxy Leader* and *MV Eternity C*—but it also substantively addresses the critical issues of environmental hazards caused by damaged vessels and the severe impediments to life-saving humanitarian assistance for the Yemeni people. Furthermore, it emphasizes the imperative of restraint, adherence to the UN Charter and international law, and the urgent necessity of addressing the root causes contributing to heightened regional tensions.

Guyana expresses its appreciation to all Council members for their constructive engagement throughout this process. We urge all members to vote in favour of this balanced and timely draft resolution.

after.Algeria:
I thank Guyana and Sierra Leone for their tireless and constructive efforts in leading the negotiations on this resolution.

Algeria voted in favour of the resolution just adopted. Our positive vote reflects our steadfast commitment to the maintenance of international peace and security, the preservation of maritime safety, the freedom of navigation, and the protection of innocent seafarers in the Red Sea and surrounding waterways. Algeria reiterates its firm condemnation of attacks against commercial and merchant vessels.

As the Council is aware, Algeria abstained on resolutions 2722 (2024), 2739 (2024), 2768 (2025), and 2787 (2025). Our abstentions were driven by profound concerns regarding the misinterpretation and abuse of Council resolutions to justify military strikes on the sovereign territory of Yemen under the pretext of self-defence, as well as the persistent failure to address the regional root causes driving these escalations.

The text adopted today, however, marks important and necessary progress in addressing those concerns. We commend the co-sponsors for including clear language affirming that Security Council resolutions must not be misinterpreted or abused, and emphasizing that any actions undertaken to protect maritime navigation must strictly conform to international law and respect the sovereignty, unity, and territorial integrity of Yemen and all coastal States in the region. We also welcome the recognition that the primary responsibility for maritime security rests with the littoral States, as well as the acknowledgement of the need to address root causes contributing to regional tensions.

Algeria reaffirms that security in the Red Sea cannot be treated in a vacuum. Sustainable maritime security and de-escalation across the wider region require addressing the fundamental root causes of instability, foremost among them the devastating situation in Gaza. Lasting peace demands the full, unconditional respect for international law, the UN Charter, and the end of all actions that threaten regional stability.

I thank you.
after.China:
China abstained in the voting on the draft resolution just adopted. I would like to elaborate on China’s position.

First, the Red Sea is an important international corridor for the transport of goods and energy. For some time now, the Houthis have continued their attacks on commercial vessels in the Red Sea and adjacent waters, threatening the safety of international navigation routes, disrupting the normal order of international trade, and impacting regional peace and stability. China expresses its grave concern over this. China has consistently called for an immediate cessation of attacks on civilian and commercial vessels and for respecting the navigational rights of commercial vessels of all countries in accordance with international law, in order to safeguard the safety and security of shipping lanes in the Red Sea.

Secondly, China has always maintained that the Security Council's resolutions must not be misinterpreted or abused. Since the adoption of resolution 2722 (2024), certain countries have launched military strikes against Yemen, which have not eliminated the threats to shipping, but have instead aggravated tensions in the Red Sea, inflicted casualties and damage on civilian infrastructure, and complicated the Yemeni political process. Military means cannot resolve the dilemma in the Red Sea; on the contrary, they only risk wider regional escalation. The sovereignty, security, and territorial integrity of Yemen and all littoral States must be earnestly respected.

Thirdly, the current tensions in the Red Sea are a prominent spillover of the broader Middle East conflict. Only by addressing the root causes, realizing an immediate and durable ceasefire in Gaza, and de-escalating regional conflicts can we fundamentally restore peace and tranquility to the Red Sea. We call on all parties concerned to exercise restraint, cease actions that escalate tensions, and work together toward political and diplomatic solutions.

China appreciates the efforts made by the co-sponsors, Guyana and Sierra Leone, to accommodate the concerns of various parties during the consultations on the draft resolution. However, in view of our consistent position on resolution 2722 (2024) and its subsequent extensions, China felt compelled to abstain in the voting. China stands ready to work with the international community to continue to play a constructive role in promoting the de-escalation of tensions in the Red Sea and advancing the political settlement of the Yemeni issue.

Thank you, Mr. President.
after.Denmark:
Denmark voted in favour of this resolution, and we warmly welcome its adoption today. We thank the delegations of Guyana and Sierra Leone for their constructive leadership and tireless efforts in steering these negotiations.

As a major maritime nation, Denmark attaches the utmost importance to the preservation of freedom of navigation, maritime safety, and the rules-based international order, as reflected in the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea. The ongoing, unlawful Houthi attacks against commercial and merchant vessels in the Red Sea and adjacent waters continue to pose a direct and severe threat to the lives of innocent seafarers, to global supply chains, and to the marine environment.

We welcome that the Council has once again spoken clearly in condemning these reckless attacks and demanding their immediate cessation. We particularly welcome the resolution's demand for the immediate and unconditional release of the crew of the *Galaxy Leader*, the crew of the *Eternity C*, and all other unlawfully detained mariners. The safety, security, and well-being of seafarers must remain paramount.

Furthermore, we underscore the vital importance of strictly enforcing the targeted arms embargo pursuant to resolution 2216 (2015). The international community must redouble its efforts to stop the flow of weapons and military materiel that enable the Houthis to carry out these unacceptable attacks.

Extending the Secretary-General’s reporting mandate through July 2026 ensures that the Council remains actively seized of this critical matter. Denmark will continue to stand firmly with its international partners to protect maritime routes, uphold international law, and ensure the safety of global navigation.
after.France:
*(spoke in French)*

France welcomes the adoption of the resolution submitted by Guyana and Sierra Leone, extending the Secretary-General’s reporting mandate on the situation in the Red Sea. We voted in favour of this text because it reaffirms essential principles to which France remains deeply committed.

The ongoing attacks perpetrated by the Houthis against commercial and merchant vessels in the Red Sea and adjacent waters are unacceptable. They directly threaten the safety of seafarers, international navigation, global trade, and the marine environment. France condemns these destabilizing attacks in the strongest terms and once again demands that the Houthis cease them immediately. We also reiterate our call for the immediate and unconditional release of the *Galaxy Leader* and its crew, as well as all unlawfully detained seafarers.

In accordance with international law, in particular the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, freedom of navigation and maritime security must be guaranteed. It is in this spirit that France, alongside its European partners within operation EUNAVFOR ASPIDES, contributes actively and responsibly to the protection of merchant vessels and the defense of navigational rights in the region.

Finally, France recalls the crucial need for all States to strictly implement the targeted arms embargo established by resolution 2216 (2015). The flow of weapons and military materiel to the Houthis must end. We urge all regional and international actors to exercise restraint in order to prevent further regional escalation and to ensure the unhindered delivery of vital humanitarian assistance to the Yemeni people.
after.Greece:
Greece welcomes the adoption of today’s resolution, and we express our sincere appreciation to the delegations of Guyana and Sierra Leone for their leadership and constructive efforts in bringing this text forward. 

As a premier maritime nation and a staunch advocate of international law, including the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), Greece has consistently maintained that the maintenance of maritime security and the unimpeded exercise of navigational rights and freedoms in the Red Sea and surrounding waterways are vital for global trade, energy security, and international peace and stability. 

The ongoing, reckless attacks by the Houthis against commercial and merchant vessels must stop immediately. These attacks constitute an unacceptable disruption to global supply chains and trade routes, create severe risks of environmental catastrophe in a fragile marine ecosystem, and, above all, endanger the lives of innocent seafarers. As we have repeatedly stressed, there can be no justification whatsoever for targeting commercial shipping or imperiling the men and women who serve international maritime trade. In this regard, we reiterate our urgent call for the immediate and unconditional release of the *MV Galaxy Leader*, the crew of the *MV Eternity C*, and all other unlawfully detained seafarers.

We also underscore the critical importance of strictly adhering to the targeted arms embargo established under resolution 2216 (2015), as cutting off the illicit flow of weapons and materiel to the Houthis is indispensable for restoring stability.

By extending the reporting mandate under resolution 2722 (2024) through 15 July 2026, the Security Council sends a clear and persistent signal that the international community remains vigilant and committed to safeguarding freedom of navigation. Greece will continue to work tirelessly alongside all partners to ensure maritime security, protect international law, and promote regional peace.

I thank you.
after.Pakistan:
Pakistan voted in favour of the resolution just adopted, reaffirming our principled commitment to the maintenance of international peace and security, the preservation of freedom of navigation, and the safety of maritime commercial shipping.

In line with Pakistan’s consistent position, we condemn all attacks against commercial and merchant vessels navigating the Red Sea and adjacent waterways. These vital maritime corridors represent critical lifelines for global trade and energy supplies, as well as crucial conduits for the delivery of humanitarian aid to the people of Yemen and the wider region. The safety and security of commercial mariners must be safeguarded, and we reiterate our call for the immediate and unconditional release of all unlawfully detained crew members.

At the same time, we emphasize that any response to threats against maritime navigation must strictly conform to international law, including the Charter of the United Nations, and must fully respect the sovereignty, unity, and territorial integrity of Yemen and of all littoral and coastal States in the region. Security Council resolutions must not be misinterpreted or used as justification for unilateral military actions that risk further escalation.

Furthermore, we must not lose sight of the broader regional dynamics. As we have repeatedly stressed, restoring lasting peace and maritime security in the Red Sea cannot be achieved in isolation from addressing the underlying root causes of regional instability. A comprehensive and durable cessation of hostilities in the wider region, including an immediate end to the conflict in Gaza, remains indispensable to preventing dangerous regional spillover and achieving lasting stability.

We hope that the extension of the Secretary-General’s reporting mandate will continue to provide the Council with objective assessments, and we urge all parties to exercise maximum restraint and pursue diplomatic avenues to de-escalate tensions and secure sustainable peace.

I thank you.
after.Panama:
Panama voted in favour of the resolution just adopted, and we thank the delegations of Guyana and Sierra Leone for their leadership, balanced approach, and constructive engagement in penning and facilitating this text.

As a major maritime nation, the world’s leading ship registry, and the administrator of the Panama Canal, Panama reiterates its unwavering commitment to the freedom of navigation, maritime security, and the strict observance of international law, particularly the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea. 

The continued attacks against commercial and merchant vessels in the Red Sea and surrounding waterways constitute a direct and unacceptable threat to global commerce, the safety of maritime transit routes, and international supply chains. Crucially, these unlawful attacks directly jeopardize the lives and safety of innocent seafarers who sustain global trade. Panama underscores the demand for the immediate and unconditional release of the crew of the *Galaxy Leader*, as well as all other unlawfully detained seafarers, and calls on all parties to respect the humanitarian and labor rights of maritime workers.

Furthermore, we stress the grave risks that such reckless attacks pose to the marine environment, regional security, and the delivery of vital humanitarian assistance to populations in need, including the people of Yemen. 

The Security Council has a clear responsibility to maintain international peace and security and to protect freedom of navigation. By extending the Secretary-General’s reporting mandate through July 2026, the Council ensures that it remains actively and effectively seized of the situation. Panama calls on all parties to strictly respect the Charter of the United Nations, international law, and Council resolutions, and to refrain from actions that could further escalate tensions in this vital maritime corridor.
after.Republic of Korea:
The Republic of Korea voted in favour of the resolution just adopted. 

First, I would like to express our appreciation to the co-penholders—Guyana and Sierra Leone—for their dedicated efforts in steering the consultations and presenting this balanced and timely text.

As a peninsular nation surrounded by the sea on three sides and heavily reliant on international maritime trade, the Republic of Korea has a vital stake in safeguarding freedom of navigation and maritime security. The Red Sea is one of the world's most critical sea routes, and lawful commercial transit must be preserved without disruption.

Attacks by the Houthis against commercial and merchant vessels are unacceptable and unjustifiable under any circumstances. They endanger the lives of innocent seafarers, destabilize global supply chains, and pose serious ecological threats to the marine environment. We reiterate our call for the immediate cessation of all such attacks, as well as the immediate and unconditional release of the *MV Galaxy Leader*, its crew, and all other unlawfully detained mariners.

We also underscore the critical importance of full compliance with the targeted arms embargo established pursuant to resolution 2216 (2015). Preventing the illicit flow of weapons and advanced military materiel to the Houthis is essential to halting further maritime attacks and de-escalating regional tensions.

Today's adoption sends a clear, united signal that the Security Council remains actively engaged on this crucial matter. The Republic of Korea hopes that the extension of the reporting mandate through July 2026 will contribute to sustained international monitoring and help restore stability and security in the Red Sea.

I thank you.
after.Russian Federation:
The Russian Federation abstained in the voting on the draft resolution submitted by Guyana and Sierra Leone on the situation in the Red Sea.

We certainly appreciate the efforts of the co-sponsors to inject greater balance into the text, including by incorporating language urging restraint, emphasizing respect for international law, sovereignty and territorial integrity, and explicitly warning against the misinterpretation or abuse of Security Council resolutions.

At the same time, this document remains fundamentally tethered to notorious resolution 2722 (2024) and its subsequent iterations, against which we have consistently raised serious objections. Our principled position on the issue of maritime security in the Red Sea is well known: we advocate unreservedly for the safety and freedom of international navigation and condemn attacks on commercial vessels and the unlawful detention of seafarers. However, we cannot overlook the fact that the framework established under resolution 2722 (2024) continues to be weaponized by the United States and the United Kingdom to provide a pseudo-legal cover for their ongoing, unprovoked strikes against the territory of the sovereign State of Yemen.

These aggressive actions by the Western coalition, undertaken without any mandate from the Security Council, constitute a flagrant violation of the Charter of the United Nations and international law. Far from securing maritime routes, this military campaign has only further militarized the Red Sea, fueled dangerous regional escalation, and undermined efforts toward a peaceful settlement in Yemen. We must reiterate in no uncertain terms: the Security Council has never authorized, and does not authorize, the use of force against the sovereign territory of Yemen, and attempts to interpret the Council’s resolutions as a license for unilateral military ventures are completely unacceptable.

Moreover, it remains impossible to separate the crisis in the Red Sea from the broader regional catastrophe, the core of which is the unresolved Palestinian-Israeli conflict and the ongoing devastation in the Gaza Strip. Genuine stabilization of the waterways of the Middle East cannot be achieved through bombs and missile strikes. It requires addressing root causes, an immediate and unconditional ceasefire in Gaza, and the pursuit of political and diplomatic solutions that respect the sovereignty and interests of all States in the region.
after.Sierra Leone:
Sierra Leone welcomes the adoption of today’s resolution, which we had the honour of co-sponsoring alongside Guyana. We express our appreciation to Guyana for its constructive leadership during the drafting and negotiation process, and to all Council members for their constructive engagement that made the adoption of this resolution possible.

Sierra Leone’s position on this agenda item has been consistent and principled. The Security Council must speak with a clear voice to protect maritime security, navigational rights, and the freedom of navigation for all vessels, in full accordance with international law, including the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea. The ongoing attacks against commercial and merchant vessels in the Red Sea and surrounding waterways not only disrupt vital global supply chains and increase costs for international commerce, but also pose grave risks to the lives and safety of innocent seafarers and threaten the fragile marine environment.

We reiterate our condemnation of these attacks and demand their immediate cessation, as well as the unconditional release of all unlawfully detained crew members, including those of the *Galaxy Leader* and the *Eternity C*. At the same time, we emphasize that any measures taken to defend navigational rights must strictly conform to international law and the Charter of the United Nations, fully respecting the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Yemen and coastal States in the region.

We also underscore the critical importance of de-escalation, restraint, and the unhindered delivery of humanitarian assistance to the Yemeni people. A lasting solution requires urgently addressing the root causes contributing to broader regional tensions and advancing an inclusive Yemeni-led, Yemeni-owned peace process.

By extending the Secretary-General’s reporting mandate under resolution 2722 (2024) through July 15, 2026, the Council ensures that it remains credibly informed and actively seized of these developments. It is for these reasons that Sierra Leone co-sponsored and voted in favour of the resolution.

I thank you.
after.Slovenia:
Slovenia welcomes the adoption of the resolution today and thanks the co-penholders, Guyana and Sierra Leone, for their dedicated efforts to achieve broad support across the Council.

As a maritime country, with the Port of Koper serving as a critical commercial gateway, freedom of navigation and the safety of maritime sea lanes are of vital importance to Slovenia. We continue to unequivocally condemn the ongoing Houthi attacks against commercial and merchant vessels in the Red Sea and surrounding waters. These reckless attacks violate international law, including the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, endanger innocent seafarers, disrupt international supply chains, and threaten global food security and humanitarian relief. We reiterate our demand for the immediate cessation of all such attacks and for the immediate and unconditional release of the *Galaxy Leader* and its crew, as well as all unlawfully detained seafarers.

We particularly welcome the inclusion in today's resolution of language addressing the severe environmental and ecological risks posed by attacks on commercial vessels. As we have repeatedly warned in this chamber, an environmental catastrophe in the fragile marine ecosystem of the Red Sea would have devastating and long-lasting consequences for coastal communities and the entire region. We are pleased to see this Council finally reflect that reality and call for concerted efforts to mitigate maritime environmental threats.

At the same time, we underline that all measures taken to defend vessels and protect freedom of navigation must strictly adhere to international law, including the Charter of the United Nations and international humanitarian law. De-escalation, regional stability, and the pursuit of a comprehensive political settlement in Yemen remain essential. 

By extending the Secretary-General’s reporting mandate through July 2026, the Council ensures that it remains actively engaged and informed on this pressing issue.

I thank you.
after.Somalia:
Somalia voted in favour of the resolution just adopted, co-sponsored by Guyana and Sierra Leone, extending the reporting mandate under resolution 2722 (2024).

As a nation deeply invested in the security and stability of the Red Sea and surrounding waterways, our vote today reflects our steadfast commitment to maritime security, which remains vital both to our region and to global commerce and stability. We remain gravely concerned by the ongoing attacks against commercial and merchant vessels in the Red Sea and adjacent waters, and by their far-reaching economic, humanitarian, security, and environmental ramifications.

This resolution represents a necessary and constructive step. However, its effective implementation requires careful consideration of regional dynamics and sensitivities. Maritime security in the Red Sea is inextricably linked to the stability of its coastal States and the broader pursuit of peace across the region. Lasting solutions can only be achieved by addressing the root causes of instability and conflict, while fully respecting the sovereignty, unity, and territorial integrity of all States in the region.

Somalia reiterates that the primary responsibility for ensuring maritime security and stability in the Red Sea rests with its coastal and littoral States, supported by constructive international cooperation. We must continue to pursue diplomatic avenues, exercise utmost restraint to prevent further regional escalation, and ensure that the Red Sea remains a safe and secure corridor for international navigation, peace, and shared prosperity.
after.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort:
The United Kingdom welcomes the adoption of this resolution and thanks Guyana and Sierra Leone for their leadership and constructive efforts in bringing this text forward.

The United Kingdom continues to condemn in the strongest possible terms the illegal, dangerous, and reckless attacks by the Houthis against commercial and merchant shipping in the Red Sea and adjacent waters. These attacks threaten the safety of innocent seafarers, disrupt critical global supply chains, drive up the cost of food and essential goods, and endanger the fragile marine environment. 

By adopting this resolution today, the Security Council has sent a clear and unified message that these attacks must cease immediately. We also reiterate our demand for the immediate and unconditional release of the *Galaxy Leader* and its crew, as well as all other unlawfully detained mariners. 

The United Kingdom reaffirms the right of Member States, in accordance with international law, to defend vessels from attacks. We also emphasize the vital necessity of strict compliance with the targeted arms embargo established under resolution 2216 (2015), and we urge all States to prevent the supply of weapons and materiel that fuel these illicit activities.

Extending the Secretary-General’s reporting mandate through July 2026 will ensure that this Council remains fully informed and actively seized of the threat posed to international maritime security. The United Kingdom remains steadfastly committed to defending freedom of navigation, upholding international law, and restoring security and stability to these vital international waterways.

I thank you.
after.United States of America:
Thank you, Mr. President.

The United States voted in favor of today’s resolution, which sends a clear and united message that the Security Council will not stand by as the Houthis continue their reckless and unlawful attacks on international shipping in the Red Sea and surrounding waterways. We thank Guyana and Sierra Leone for their leadership in facilitating this resolution.

For over two years, the Houthis have flagrantly disregarded the Council’s unequivocal demands, starting with resolution 2722 (2024), to cease all attacks against commercial and merchant vessels. These unprovoked attacks endanger innocent mariners, disrupt global supply chains, drive up the costs of food and vital humanitarian assistance, and pose grave environmental risks to the delicate marine ecosystems of the Red Sea. 

Today’s resolution rightly reaffirms the Council’s condemnation of these attacks, takes note of the right of Member States to defend their vessels from attack in accordance with international law, and extends the Secretary-General’s vital reporting mandate through July 15, 2026. This reporting remains essential to ensuring the Council is provided with accurate, timely information on the scale and nature of these attacks and the weapons used to conduct them.

Furthermore, we welcome the Council’s renewed demand for the immediate and unconditional release of the *MV Galaxy Leader* and its crew, as well as the crew of the *MV Eternity C* and all other unlawfully detained seafarers. The Houthis must end their hostage-taking and respect the rights of civilian mariners.

Finally, we must address the root driver of this crisis: the Islamic Republic of Iran. The Houthis could not sustain these complex and sophisticated attacks without Iran’s continuous provision of advanced weaponry, intelligence, and technical support—all in direct violation of the targeted arms embargo established by resolution 2216 (2015). Today’s resolution reaffirms that all Member States must strictly adhere to their arms embargo obligations. The international community cannot allow Iran to continue destabilizing the region with impunity.

The United States remains steadfast in working alongside our allies and international partners to defend freedom of navigation, protect international commerce, and hold the Houthis and their Iranian backers accountable.

Thank you, Mr. President.
